title: A workspace or a group of workspaces can be put to sleep and woken
body:
When the server stops, `save.rs` writes each workspace's layout, and on the next start the panes come back empty and pinned terminals restart in their saved directories. Programs in panes cost memory and CPU while their workspace sits unused, and today the only way to free that is to close the workspace or stop the server.

## Proposal

Sleeping a workspace puts it in the state a server stop would leave it in, while the server and the other workspaces keep running:

- Sleep saves the workspace's layout, asks its windows to close, and kills the programs decade started in it. The panes stay, empty.
- A sleeping workspace shows its empty panes with a wake button. Switching to it does not wake it.
- Wake runs the restore path for that one workspace: pinned terminals restart in their saved directories.
- A sleeping workspace stays asleep when the server restarts. The save file gains a flag for it, which bumps the format's version byte, and the reader keeps an arm for the old layout.
- Sleeping a workspace whose agent is working asks first.
- A group's right-click menu offers Sleep and Wake for every workspace in it.

## Cost

Sleep is as good as restore. Shells come back fresh, without scrollback or what ran in them. An agent session in a pane comes back only with decade-cf942a, and GUI apps only with decade-15e5eb.

## Rejected

- Freezing with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT. It wakes instantly with everything intact, but frees no memory unless the system swaps, and network connections such as an agent's may time out while stopped. Jack chose not to take it on now.

## Decided on 2026-11-21

- A sleeping workspace's card shows a Zzz button, and a click on it wakes the workspace.
- A sleeping workspace's right-click menu offers Wake, and a group's menu offers Wake for its workspaces.
- A workspace never sleeps by itself.

Jack answered the design questions on 2026-11-21.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/8a3a6cd2
notes.text:
Jack signed off this plan on 2026-11-22. It lands as two commits on `dev`.

1. Server side. Sleep takes the workspace's `Saved` record before anything dies, kills the programs decade started in it, asks its other windows to close, drops its agents, point and flash, and replaces its tabs with what `Saved::workspace()` builds from that record. The result matches what a server restart shows, and `prune` never sees the collapse. `Children` tags each child with its workspace id so one workspace's programs can be killed. Wake runs `start_workspace()` with the stored terminal tabs. The save format goes to version 5 with `sleeping` on `Saved`, and the reader keeps parsing versions 2 to 4. A workspace restored asleep spawns no terminals.
2. Interface. A sleeping card shows Zzz in its round button, and a click wakes it. A sleeping tile is dimmed with a "z". Each empty pane shows "asleep" with a wake button. The workspace menu offers Sleep or Wake, and a group's menu offers "Sleep all" and "Wake all". Sleep asks for a second click while the workspace has a working agent. Switching to a sleeping workspace does not wake it.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/8a3a6cd2
notes.text: Landed in a406238 (sleep, wake and save format version 5 on the server) and f62a5f1 (card mark, tile, asleep placeholders, workspace and group menus, guards against starting programs). Scripted sessions slept and woke a split workspace and restarted the server with one asleep. A window from a process that outlives the sleep can still land in the workspace; that is filed separately.
